content: Most tobacco control programs targeting adolescents focus on preventing the initiation of smoking. However, smoking among teenagers remains prevalent. It is uncertain whether interventions proven effective for adults are equally beneficial for adolescents attempting to quit smoking. This review, an update of a Cochrane Review first published in 2006, aimed to assess the effectiveness of various strategies designed to help young people stop smoking. The review included randomized controlled trials (both individually and cluster-randomized) that recruited individuals under the age of 20 who were regular tobacco smokers. Interventions evaluated included pharmacotherapy, psychosocial interventions, and complex programs targeting families, schools, or communities. Studies focused solely on preventing smoking initiation were excluded. The primary outcome was the smoking status of participants at least six months after the intervention, measured among those who were smokers at the start of the study. The search for relevant studies was conducted in June 2017 using the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group's Specialized Register, which includes trials identified in CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies and extracted data. The included studies were evaluated for risk of bias using standard Cochrane methods. Interventions were categorized by type and theoretical basis. When meta-analysis was feasible, pooled risk ratios (RRs) were calculated using the Mantel-Haenszel fixed-effect method, based on quit rates at six months' follow-up. A total of 41 trials, involving over 13,000 young participants, met the inclusion criteria. These included 26 individually randomized controlled trials and 15 cluster-randomized trials. Most studies were judged to have a high or unclear risk of bias in at least one domain. The interventions varied widely, with the majority involving individual or group counseling, often supplemented with self-help materials to create complex interventions. Eight studies primarily utilized computer-based or messaging interventions, while four small studies evaluated pharmacological treatments, such as nicotine patches, nicotine gum, or bupropion. The findings indicated evidence of an effect for group counseling interventions (9 studies; RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.77). However, there was no evidence of effectiveness for individual counseling (7 studies; RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.39), mixed delivery methods (8 studies; RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.66), or computer/messaging interventions (pooled RRs between 0.79 and 1.18 across 9 studies). Pharmacological interventions showed no clear evidence of effectiveness, with wide confidence intervals (nicotine replacement therapy: 3 studies; RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.48 to 2.58; bupropion: 1 study; RR 1.49, 95% CI 0.55 to 4.02). No subgroup analysis ruled out the possibility of a clinically meaningful effect. Adverse events related to pharmacological treatments were reported in some studies, though most were mild. In contrast, no adverse events were reported in studies of behavioral interventions. The certainty of the evidence for all comparisons was rated as low or very low, primarily due to clinical heterogeneity of the interventions, imprecision in effect size estimates, and concerns about risk of bias. In conclusion, there is limited evidence to suggest that either behavioral support or smoking cessation medications significantly increase the proportion of young people who quit smoking in the long term. Group-based behavioral interventions appear to be the most promising, but the evidence remains limited for all types of interventions. There is a continued need for well-designed, adequately powered randomized controlled trials to evaluate interventions for this population of smokers.
